overview:
Bhadrabāhu (often styled Ācārya Bhadrabāhu or Ārya Bhadrabāhu) occupies a pivotal yet historically complex place in Jain memory. Both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions revere him as the last śruta-kevalin—the final monk said to possess complete mastery of the fourteen Pūrvas, an early and now‑lost corpus of Jain scriptural knowledge. In sectarian lists of pontiffs he appears as a crucial link between the age of Mahāvīra’s direct disciples and the later, more fragmented community, and his name is closely associated with the migration of monks during a great famine and with the eventual differentiation of Digambara and Śvetāmbara lineages.

Traditional accounts place Bhadrabāhu’s life in the 4th–3rd centuries BCE, with birth in the region of Puṇḍravardhana in eastern India and death at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa in present‑day Karnataka. Digambara narratives often describe him as born into a Brahmin family and emphasize his prodigious intellect and early attraction to Jain teachings, though these details come from later hagiographical texts rather than contemporary inscriptions. In the Digambara lineage of śruta‑kevalins, he is usually counted as the fifth and last, following Viṣṇu, Nandimitra, Aparājita, and Govardhana; Śvetāmbara sources also acknowledge his status as a śruta‑kevalin but differ on some points of teacher‑disciple relationships and monastic classification.

A central episode in Bhadrabāhu’s remembered life is his prophecy of a twelve‑year famine in Magadha. According to many Jain narratives, he foresaw the impending calamity and led a large group of monks southward from Pāṭaliputra to the region around Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa. In Digambara retellings, the Mauryan emperor Candragupta, having adopted Jainism, abdicated his throne and accompanied Bhadrabāhu as a disciple, eventually undertaking the fast of sallekhanā and dying at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa after his teacher’s death. Epigraphic material from Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa confirms an early Jain presence and commemorates Bhadrabāhu and Candragupta together, but modern scholarship notes that the detailed narrative of their relationship is shaped by later sectarian and devotional elaboration rather than independent historical records.

The famine migration is also linked to the gradual division of the Jain saṅgha. When the group associated with Bhadrabāhu is said to have returned north after the famine, they reportedly found that monks under the leadership of Sthūlabhadra had begun to wear white cloth and had convened a council at Pāṭaliputra to collect and edit the scriptures. Those who maintained the older practice of nudity and rejected the council’s textual decisions eventually came to be known as Digambaras (“sky‑clad”), while those who accepted clothing and the emerging canon became Śvetāmbaras (“white‑clad”). Although the historical process of sectarian formation was gradual and multi‑layered, Bhadrabāhu’s figure stands at the symbolic center of this “great schism” in many traditional narratives.

Śvetāmbara tradition further associates Bhadrabāhu with the Kalpa Sūtra, a key text recited during Paryuṣaṇa that includes biographies of Tīrthaṅkaras and a Sthavirāvalī (succession list of monastic leaders). In these lists, Bhadrabāhu appears as a major pontiff whose disciples founded important monastic lineages, especially in eastern India. Digambara sources, by contrast, focus less on textual authorship and more on his role as a guardian of the Pūrvas and as the spiritual guide of Candragupta. Modern historians, working with both northern and southern textual traditions and with inscriptions from Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa and elsewhere, emphasize that Bhadrabāhu is an “elusive” figure: highly revered, but known through sources that are late, sectarian, and sometimes mutually contradictory.

In contemporary Jain studies, Bhadrabāhu is therefore approached through layered evidence: early Śvetāmbara pontifical lists, Digambara narrative and doctrinal texts, and epigraphic records from Karnataka. These materials agree on his importance as a śruta‑kevalin and leader of the saṅgha, but they diverge on details of his teacher, disciples, and precise role in the famine migration and sectarian split. For practicing Jains, he remains a symbol of scriptural mastery, foresight in times of crisis, and the continuity of the tradition from Mahāvīra’s era into the age of imperial polities. For historians, he illustrates how memory, devotion, and regional transmission shape the remembered lives of early Jain ācāryas.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa Sūtra (including Sthavirāvalī)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu in Śvetāmbara tradition
primary_sources.translation: The Kalpa Sūtra is a Śvetāmbara canonical text recited especially during Paryuṣaṇa. It contains biographies of Tīrthaṅkaras, including Mahāvīra, and a Sthavirāvalī—a succession list of monastic leaders from Sudharmasvāmin onward. In these lists, Bhadrabāhu is named among the principal ācāryas who transmit the teaching and ordain further disciples.
primary_sources.notes: Corpus tier A/B. The attribution of authorship to Bhadrabāhu is accepted in Śvetāmbara tradition but treated cautiously in modern scholarship, which notes the difficulty of assigning individual authorship to early canonical compilations. The Sthavirāvalī material is an important early witness to his place in the northern pontifical lineage, though exact wording and sequence vary across manuscripts and recensions.

primary_sources.title: Paryuṣaṇa‑kalpa and related Sthavirāvalī traditions
primary_sources.author: Anonymous Śvetāmbara compilers
primary_sources.translation: In the Paryuṣaṇa‑kalpa and associated liturgical texts, Bhadrabāhu appears in the evolving Sthavirāvalī as a major pontiff. Later phases of the list mention his disciples Godāsa, Agnidatta, Yajñadatta, and Somadatta, and trace the emergence of the Godāsa‑gaṇa and its branches linked to eastern Indian centers such as Tāmraliptikā and Pauṇḍravardhanikā.
primary_sources.notes: Corpus tier A/B. These materials are among the earliest northern textual witnesses to Bhadrabāhu’s disciples and to the spread of Jain monastic lineages into Bengal and surrounding regions. The lists are partly liturgical and partly historical, and modern scholars caution that they reflect both memory and later systematization of pontifical succession.

primary_sources.title: Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa inscriptions (Bhadrabāhu–Candragupta tradition)
primary_sources.author: Various donors and scribes (Prakrit and early Kannada inscriptions)
primary_sources.translation: Inscriptions at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa commemorate Bhadrabāhu and Candragupta together, referring to the site as a place of their austerities and death. They present Bhadrabāhu as a revered ācārya and Candragupta as a royal disciple who undertook severe penance and the fast of sallekhanā under Jain guidance.
primary_sources.notes: Corpus tier A. These inscriptions provide the strongest early epigraphic support for associating Bhadrabāhu with Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa and with a royal disciple, though they do not supply the full narrative found in later literary sources. Modern historians use them as anchors for reconstructing the spread of Jainism into Karnataka and for assessing the historicity of the Bhadrabāhu–Candragupta story.

primary_sources.title: Digambara narrative texts (e.g., Ārādhanā of Śivārya, Tiloyapaṇṇatti, Harivaṃśa‑purāṇa)
primary_sources.author: Śivārya, Yativṛṣabha, Jinasena and other Digambara authors
primary_sources.translation: These texts, composed in Prakrit, Sanskrit, and later regional languages, include narrative and doctrinal passages that present Bhadrabāhu as the last śruta‑kevalin, the spiritual preceptor of Candragupta, and the leader of the famine migration from Magadha to the south. They emphasize his mastery of the Pūrvas and his role in preserving the tradition during a time of crisis.
primary_sources.notes: Corpus tier B/C. While not contemporaneous with Bhadrabāhu, these works are central to the Digambara memory of his life and status. They blend doctrinal exposition with hagiography, and modern scholarship reads them critically alongside northern sources and inscriptions to reconstruct a more balanced historical picture.

primary_sources.title: Northern commentarial works (e.g., Uttarādhyayana‑niryukti, Āvasyaka‑cūrṇi, works of Haribhadra and Hemacandra)
primary_sources.author: Bhadrabāhu (niryuktis, according to tradition), later commentators such as Haribhadra Sūri and Hemacandra
primary_sources.translation: These texts refer to Bhadrabāhu in passing, often in the context of pontifical lists, doctrinal discussions, or narrative exempla. They reinforce his image as a śruta‑kevalin and as a key figure in the transmission of doctrine, while sometimes differing from southern sources on details such as his preceptor and the names of his disciples.
primary_sources.notes: Corpus tier B/C. The references are fragmentary but important for tracing how Bhadrabāhu was remembered in the Śvetāmbara scholastic tradition. They also illustrate the gradual layering of biographical detail over an originally sparse historical core.

misconceptions.myth: Bhadrabāhu is a fully historically documented figure whose life story is known in detail and without dispute.
misconceptions.reality: Bhadrabāhu is highly revered, but the surviving evidence is late, sectarian, and sometimes contradictory. Inscriptions confirm his importance and early Jain presence in Karnataka, yet many biographical details—such as precise dates, family background, and the full narrative of his relationship with Candragupta—come from later hagiographical and doctrinal texts and are interpreted cautiously by modern historians.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain traditions agree that Bhadrabāhu authored the Kalpa Sūtra and that this authorship is a simple historical fact.
misconceptions.reality: Śvetāmbara tradition commonly attributes the Kalpa Sūtra to Bhadrabāhu and integrates him into its canonical and liturgical framework. Digambara sources do not emphasize this authorship, and modern scholarship notes that early Jain scriptures were compiled over time by multiple hands. The attribution reflects sectarian memory and reverence rather than universally accepted or easily verifiable historical authorship.

misconceptions.myth: The famine migration led by Bhadrabāhu instantly and definitively created the Digambara and Śvetāmbara sects in a single event.
misconceptions.reality: Traditional narratives place Bhadrabāhu at the center of a great famine and subsequent migration, and they link the return of his group to disagreements over nudity and scriptural councils. However, historians understand the formation of Digambara and Śvetāmbara communities as a gradual process extending over several centuries, with multiple regional and doctrinal factors. Bhadrabāhu’s story is an important symbolic episode, not a complete explanation of sectarian history.

misconceptions.myth: The detailed story of Candragupta Maurya renouncing his throne, following Bhadrabāhu to Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, and undertaking sallekhanā is fully corroborated by non‑Jain historical sources.
misconceptions.reality: The association of Candragupta with Bhadrabāhu and Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa is strongly preserved in Jain tradition and supported in outline by inscriptions that mention both figures. Yet the rich narrative of their relationship—especially the specifics of Candragupta’s renunciation and death—is not independently confirmed by contemporary non‑Jain texts. Scholars treat it as a significant Jain memory with historical elements, shaped by later devotional and sectarian concerns.

misconceptions.myth: There is only one, universally agreed‑upon Bhadrabāhu in Jain history, and all references clearly point to the same person.
misconceptions.reality: Jain sources sometimes distinguish between Bhadrabāhu I and later figures also bearing the name, and northern and southern traditions differ on aspects of his lineage and disciples. Modern researchers carefully separate these layers and caution against assuming that every mention of “Bhadrabāhu” in later texts refers to the same historical individual without contextual analysis.
